claim.pdf_says:
14.9.34.2 General format

RETURN file-name-1 RECORD [ INTO identifier-1 ]
   AT END imperative-statement-1
   [ NOT AT END imperative-statement-2 ]
   [ END-RETURN ]

(printed underlining, verified at 300 dpi: RETURN, INTO, END, NOT, END, END-RETURN are underlined; RECORD and both occurrences of AT are NOT underlined)
claim.markdown_says:
### 14.9.34.2 General format

`RETURN` file-name-1 `RECORD` [ `INTO` identifier-1 ]
   `AT` `END` imperative-statement-1
   [ `NOT` `AT` `END` imperative-statement-2 ]
   [ `END-RETURN` ]

(no "Figure notes (...)" blockquote follows the figure)
claim.why_it_matters: The figure is transcribed with a code-span-per-reserved-word convention that renders underlined and non-underlined words identically, then omits the compensating "Figure notes" blockquote the rest of the transcription uses (cf. the REWRITE general format at 14.9.35.2, whose notes read "`RECORD`, `WITH`, and `KEY` are **not** underlined — they are optional words"). Per 5.2.6.2/5.2.6.3 a non-underlined reserved word is an OPTIONAL word. As transcribed, RECORD and both AT occurrences read as required, so an implementer working from the markdown would reject the legal forms `RETURN sm-file`, `RETURN sm-file RECORD END imp-stmt`, and `NOT END imp-stmt-2` — the same falsely-restrictive drift this transcription is known for.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED by independent pixel measurement, not by eye. Rendered E:/Temp/specrecon/v738/spec_p738.png at 300 dpi (2550x3300) and ran a row/column ink profile over the general-format block. Four underline rules appear as isolated horizontal ink bands below the descender gap at rows 936-937, 1009-1010, 1081-1082 and 1153-1154. Their column extents map onto glyph-run extents as follows.

Line 1 glyph runs: RETURN (271-432), file-name-1 (460-673), RECORD (699-857), '[' (886-894), INTO (922-1015), identifier-1 (1044-1254), ']' (1279-1288). Underline segments on line 1: (273-430) and (924-1014) ONLY. RETURN and INTO are underlined; RECORD has NO rule beneath it (no ink anywhere in 699-857 on the underline rows).

Line 2 glyph runs: AT (309-360), END (389-467), imperative-statement-1 (496-943). Underline segment: (391-466) ONLY. END underlined, AT NOT underlined.

Line 3 glyph runs: '[' (314-323), NOT (350-430), AT (456-507), END (535-614), imperative-statement-2 (643-1089), ']' (1115-1123). Underline segments: (352-428) and (538-612) ONLY. NOT and END underlined, AT NOT underlined.

Line 4 glyph runs: '[' (314-322), END-RETURN (350-610), ']' (638-646). Underline segment: (352-609). END-RETURN underlined.

So the claim's characterization of the printed underlining is exactly right: RETURN, INTO, END, NOT, END, END-RETURN underlined; RECORD and both AT occurrences not underlined.

The markdown side is quoted verbatim — verified against specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 30022-30026 (submodule d22c5e4a), not merely against the extracted work unit. Every reserved word sits in an identical code span, so the keyword/optional-word distinction is destroyed, and no 'Figure notes' blockquote follows.

I tried three ways to refute this and all three failed:
(1) Is the distinction preserved elsewhere in the entry? No. Syntax rule 4 mentions 'The AT END phrase and the NOT AT END phrase' but never says AT is optional; nothing in 14.9.34 recovers it.
(2) Is there a global transcription convention note declaring that code spans do not imply 'required'? No. The file has no such preamble; the transcription's ONLY mechanism for preserving underlining is the per-figure 'Figure notes' blockquote, of which there are 225 instances.
(3) Is the uniform-code-span style simply the house style here, making this formatting rather than content? No — and this is the decisive point. The two immediately adjacent statements both preserve the distinction correctly. 14.9.33.2 (RESUME, line 29961) uses a fenced block plus notes reading "`RESUME`, `NEXT`, and `STATEMENT` are underlined in the printed standard (required words); `AT` is not underlined." 14.9.35.2 (REWRITE, line 30102) reads "`RECORD`, `WITH`, and `KEY` are **not** underlined — they are optional words" — the claim quotes this accurately. 14.9.36.2 (ROLLBACK) uses an explicit `<u>ROLLBACK</u>` tag. 14.9.34.2 alone drops the information, sandwiched between neighbours that flag the very two words it loses (AT and RECORD). That is drift, not convention.

The normative consequence is real. 5.2.2 Keywords: 'shown in uppercase and underlined ... They are required'. 5.2.3 Optional words: 'shown in uppercase and not underlined ... may be written'. Restated at 8.3.2.4.2/8.3.2.4.3. As transcribed, a reader takes RECORD and AT to be required and rejects legal source.

Two defects in the claim's write-up, corrected below but not fatal to it: a mis-citation, and one bogus example form.
verdict.corrected_description:
The finding is REAL and normative, with two corrections to the reported rationale.

CORRECTION 1 — wrong section cited. The claim cites '5.2.6.2/5.2.6.3' for the rule that a non-underlined reserved word is an optional word. Those sections are Brackets and Braces respectively and say nothing about underlining. The governing sections are 5.2.2 (Keywords — 'shown in uppercase and underlined in general formats ... They are required in order to select the functionality associated with that keyword') and 5.2.3 (Optional words — 'shown in uppercase and not underlined in general formats ... may be written to add clarity'), restated normatively at 8.3.2.4.2 (Required words) and 8.3.2.4.3 (Optional words). The substance of the claim survives; only the citation is wrong.

CORRECTION 2 — one listed 'legal form' is not legal. The claim says an implementer would wrongly reject `RETURN sm-file`. That form is genuinely illegal and its rejection is correct: the 'AT END imperative-statement-1' line carries NO brackets in the printed format (confirmed by the column profile — line 2 has exactly three glyph runs, AT / END / imperative-statement-1, with none of the bracket glyphs that appear at x~314 and x~1115 on lines 3 and 4). The AT END phrase is therefore mandatory on RETURN, unlike READ. The minimum legal RETURN is `RETURN file-name-1 END imperative-statement-1`.

The surviving, correct statement of impact: because RECORD and both AT occurrences are transcribed as though required, an implementer working from the markdown would wrongly reject at least these legal forms — `RETURN sm-file END imp-stmt-1` (RECORD omitted), `RETURN sm-file RECORD END imp-stmt-1` (AT omitted), and `NOT END imp-stmt-2` (AT omitted in the NOT AT END phrase) — plus every combination thereof.

Recommended repair, matching the convention used by the neighbouring 14.9.33.2 and 14.9.35.2: re-render 14.9.34.2 as a fenced code block and append a Figure notes blockquote, e.g. '**Figure notes (RETURN statement general format).** `RETURN`, `INTO`, `END`, `NOT`, and `END-RETURN` are underlined in the printed standard (required words). `RECORD` and both occurrences of `AT` are **not** underlined — they are optional words. The AT END phrase is not bracketed and is therefore required; the NOT AT END phrase and END-RETURN are bracketed and optional. Per syntax rule 4 the AT END and NOT AT END phrases may be written in reversed order.'
